analysis.one_liner: Lets workers prove job discrimination with statistics, while employers must show each hiring rule is a business necessity.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote — it sat in a House subcommittee until the 101st Congress ended in January 1991.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have rewritten the rules of proof in employment discrimination lawsuits under Title VII of the Civil Rights Act. A worker could establish a basic case simply by showing that their group is significantly underrepresented in a job or among benefit recipients compared to the pool of qualified applicants. The employer could defeat the case only by proving that every part of its selection process was a genuine business necessity, and the bill states that it does not require or approve hiring quotas.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers and job applicants who believe they were discriminated against. They could open a case by showing a statistical gap between their group's share of a position and its share of qualified applicants, without first having to identify which specific test, credential, or requirement screened them out. The bill also promises them that no court could use it to impose quotas.

how_it_helps.text: A worker could make out a basic (prima facie) case of discrimination simply by proving their protected group is significantly less represented in the position or among benefit recipients than among qualified or likely-qualified applicants.
The employer would then have to rebut the case by proving that each part of its selection process was a business necessity — putting the burden of justification on the company rather than the worker.
The bill states that nothing in it condones or compels percentage or numerical quotas, addressing a common objection to statistical proof of discrimination.

analysis.who_pays: Employers with 15 or more employees — companies, unions, and employment agencies covered by Title VII. They would face lawsuits they could not open with statistical evidence alone, and they would bear the cost of proving that every step of their hiring, promotion, or benefits process is genuinely required by the job.

drawbacks.text: A statistics-only case could reach employers whose workforce gaps reflect factors other than discrimination, and those employers would have to litigate and justify every component of their selection process to escape liability.
Proving 'business necessity' for each part of a multi-step selection process would be a heavy and expensive burden for employers, which is the tradeoff for making the worker's initial showing easier.
The bill's own disclaimer that it does not require quotas signals that statistical proof of discrimination raised concerns about numeric hiring targets even among its backers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers, the bill would have lowered a high barrier: under the law as the courts had it in 1989, a plaintiff generally had to isolate a specific practice that caused the disparity before any burden shifted to the employer. This bill would let the disparity itself open the case, while giving employers a clear escape route (business necessity) and disclaiming quotas. The honest cost is that employers would face more litigation and would have to defend hiring tools that are common but hard to prove strictly 'necessary.' It was a genuine attempt to rebalance proof in discrimination cases, not a loophole bill, but it also never attracted support beyond its three Republican sponsors.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Education and Labor Committee and then to a subcommittee, where it sat until Congress adjourned — no committee vote, no floor vote, ever.

narrative.text: Rep. Tom Campbell of California introduced the bill on October 12, 1989, with two Republican cosponsors.
The House referred it to the Committee on Education and Labor the same day.
On November 13, 1989, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Employment Opportunities.
No further action was ever taken; the bill died in subcommittee when the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers facing discrimination lawsuits — the rules of proof stayed exactly as the courts had left them, and no version of this statistical approach ever advanced. It also meant the broader 1989-1991 fight over civil rights legislation was resolved through other bills instead of this one.

for.name: Tom Campbell
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led it as its sole original sponsor.

against.name: House Committee on Education and Labor
against.what_they_did: Took no action beyond referral — no markup or vote was ever scheduled; the bill went to a subcommittee and stayed there.

against.name: Augustus Hawkins
against.role: Chair, House Committee on Education and Labor
against.what_they_did: Chaired the committee that never brought the bill to a markup or vote during its two years in the 101st Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred to reveal a split; all three sponsors were Republicans, and the Democratic-led committee that received the bill took no action.

industries.note: If enacted, the bill would have made it far easier for workers to open discrimination cases and would have put the burden of justifying every selection step on the employer. The employer's interest in limiting liability ran directly against workers' interest in a workable path to court.
Statistics-only prima facie cases would create a broader, simpler route to bring and settle discrimination claims, expanding the market for plaintiff-side employment litigation.
